title: Kernel-driven hybrid phase partitioner to reduce latency tail while preserving throughput
creator: Marco Liu
description:
Background: Our runtime currently makes phase-splitting decisions primarily based on token count heuristics and a tenant QoS weight. As models diversify (sparse attention variants, grouped kv-cache layouts, and new kernel variants for Q4/2025 GPUs) the runtime needs a scheduler that reasons explicitly about kernel selection and attentional memory pressure when splitting prefill/decode into microphases.

Goal: Design, implement, and validate a hybrid phase partitioner that uses kernel latency/cost models and attention-memory heuristics to split prefill and decode into fragments that reduce 95th/99th latency tails without regressing overall throughput for sustained loads. The partitioner should: 1) prefer kernel-coherent fragments that reuse KV/cache layouts and specialized attention kernels; 2) avoid fragmentation that forces slow kernels mid-sequence; and 3) expose knobs for latency-first vs throughput-first service tiers.

Scope: This ticket covers the partitioning policy, kernel-cost profilers, scheduling feedback loop, unit & integration tests, and an A/B experiment in staging with two traffic mixes: short-chatty (avg tokens 40, high QPS) and long-generation (avg tokens 600, low QPS). Not in scope: packaging for Private stack upgrade or KMS changes (separate tickets).

Design sketch: 1) Offline kernel profiler: for each model variant (fp16/4-bit/1-shot sparse attention) we collect kernel latency distributions over representative sequence lengths and prefilling patterns. Output: per-kernel latency P50/P95/P99 and memory working set delta for a unit token.
2) Runtime cost model: aggregate kernel profiles into an expected cost curve given a proposed split boundary (e.g., split after prefill token N into microphase sizes M1, M2...). Cost curve includes CPU/GPU overlap benefit when contiguous kernels reuse the same kernel type and penalties when a split causes kernel switching or extra KV copy passes.
3) Partitioning policy: compute candidate splits constrained by a max fragment count and max KV scatter (to avoid excessive cache invalidation). Score candidates by latency-tail reduction per unit throughput loss. Adopt greedy-heu with simulated annealing fallback for pathological workloads.
4) Fairness and tenant isolation: integrate tenant weight and soft deadlines. For tenants with latency SLA, bias scoring towards smaller tail contribution even if throughput falls. For bulk tenants, bias towards throughput-preserving splits.
5) Dynamic feedback: runtime monitors per-fragment latencies and kernel switches; on drift from the offline model we adapt split thresholds via a lightweight controller (PID-like) with safety bounds.

Deliverables: 1) design doc (Confluence) with graphs and algorithm pseudocode; 2) kernel profiler tooling and dataset; 3) runtime implementation behind a feature flag; 4) unit + hybrid tests; 5) staging A/B experiment and dashboard showing token-level latency distribution, kernel-switch counts, and throughput; 6) roll-out plan and rollback criteria.
acceptance_criteria: Feature flagged runtime implements kernel-aware partitioner and can be toggled per-deployment
Staging A/B shows >=20% reduction in 95th latency for short-chatty traffic without >5% throughput regression
No increase in GPU memory OOMs or kv-cache corruption during experiment window
Integration tests validate kernel profiler outputs are consumed by partitioner and controller reacts to drift
Documentation (Confluence) and runbook created for rollback and tuning knobs

testing_plan: Unit: kernel-cost model unit tests with synthetic kernel profiles
Integration: end-to-end tests replaying captured traces across the feature-flagged runtime
Load: A/B on staging for two traffic mixes with 72h windows
Safety: chaos test that forces kernel failures to validate rollback and fallback to legacy partitioner
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Offline profiler mismatch with production workloads. Mitigation: conservative initial thresholds and continuous controller that tightens only when confidence grows.
Risk: Kernel-switch overhead may negate latency gains. Mitigation: explicit penalty term and max-switch budget per sequence.
Risk: Fairness regressions where bulk tenants are starved. Mitigation: unit tests for long-running tenants and quota-preserving default policy.
